explanations.explanation: Zechariah, the prophet, sees a rider and a crowd of horses in the dark, and his first move is a question: "What are these, my lord?" I think that's a smart habit, friend. When I don't understand something, I'd rather ask than guess and stamp a whole batch crooked.

The text never says Zechariah hides. The man on the horse is the one standing among the myrtle trees. Zechariah just asks, "What are these, my lord?" Me, I'd have been hiding in the flour bin, but our prophet asks his question.

explanations.answer: He runs to tell the people
explanations.explanation: No running here, friend. Zechariah asks, "What are these, my lord?" The angel who was speaking with him replies, "I will show you what they are." I think that's the better move anyway, because you can't tell people about something you haven't understood yet.

The man among the myrtle trees says, "They are the ones the LORD has sent to patrol the earth." These horses and riders go out on the LORD's sending. Later the riders report back: "We have patrolled the earth…" Think of a night watchman walking the whole neighborhood, except these riders cover the earth.

Close, but the text doesn't say the riders rule anything. The man among the myrtle trees says the LORD sent them "…to patrol the earth." Then the riders say, "We have patrolled the earth…" Patrolled is the word to hold onto, friend, and the riders use it themselves.

Judging isn't the word the man gives. He says, "They are the ones the LORD has sent to patrol the earth." The riders then report, "We have patrolled the earth…" They were sent out, and they give their report. I'd call that an honest report.

explanations.answer: How long He will withhold mercy from them
explanations.explanation: The angel of the LORD asks, "How long, O LORD of Hosts, will You withhold mercy from Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which You have been angry these seventy years?" It's a question about mercy and how long the wait will last. I think it's the kind of question you ask when the waiting has gone on a long time. Hold onto it, friend, because the very next verse has the LORD speaking kind and comforting words.

explanations.answer: When He will send the riders out to them
explanations.explanation: The riders have already been sent out, friend. They've already reported, "We have patrolled the earth…" The angel's question is about mercy for Jerusalem and the cities of Judah: "How long, O LORD of Hosts, will You withhold mercy…" So he isn't asking about the riders at all.

explanations.answer: Why the nations are so angry with them
explanations.explanation: The nations don't come up in the angel's question. He asks about the LORD's own mercy: "How long, O LORD of Hosts, will You withhold mercy from Jerusalem and the cities of Judah…" He also mentions the seventy years of the LORD's anger. It's a question aimed straight at the LORD of Hosts, not at anyone else.

Not quite, friend, because the text goes the other way. "So the LORD spoke kind and comforting words to the angel who was speaking with me." Kind and comforting is a whole different kind of reply. Nothing hard or angry is spoken to him there (Zechariah 1:13).

That's right, and it's good news. After the angel of the LORD asks how long, "…the LORD spoke kind and comforting words to the angel who was speaking with me." Nothing hard or angry is spoken to him there. The kind words go to the angel, and then the angel tells Zechariah what to proclaim.

The LORD of Hosts says it Himself: "I am very jealous for Jerusalem and Zion…" That's how He says He feels about them. After all those seventy years of waiting, I think those words land like a warm blanket. Jerusalem and Zion are on His heart.

Far away isn't what the LORD says. He says, "I am very jealous for Jerusalem and Zion…" Then He says, "I will return to Jerusalem with mercy…" (Zechariah 1:16). That's a LORD who is coming back, not one drifting off.

No tiredness in these words, friend. The LORD of Hosts says, "I am very jealous for Jerusalem and Zion…" He also says, "the LORD will again comfort Zion…" (Zechariah 1:17). Someone who's tired of you doesn't promise comfort.

True. The LORD says, "…but I am fiercely angry with the nations that are at ease." Notice the words "at ease." Those nations are sitting comfortably while Judah's story is hard. The LORD's words to Jerusalem are warm, but His words to those nations are fierce.

The text actually says it plainly: "…but I am fiercely angry with the nations that are at ease." Fiercely, friend, and that's the LORD's own word. This anger is aimed at the nations. The words for Jerusalem and Zion, a verse earlier, were different.

The LORD says, "For I was a little angry, but they have added to the calamity." The nations took a hard situation and made it harder. That's why He says He's fiercely angry with them. It's the same verse, friend, and it tells you exactly what they did.

Asking for mercy would have been a different story, and that isn't what the verse says. The LORD says, "For I was a little angry, but they have added to the calamity." The nations made things worse instead. That's what He's fiercely angry about.

Rebuilding is what the LORD Himself promises next. He says, "I will return to Jerusalem with mercy, and there My house will be rebuilt…" (Zechariah 1:16). That's not what the nations are said to do here. He says of them, "For I was a little angry, but they have added to the calamity."

The LORD says, "I will return to Jerusalem with mercy, and there My house will be rebuilt…" The word is house, and it's His house. That's a big promise to hear after seventy years. I think I'd be hugging my own oven mitts.

Gates are a reasonable guess for a city, but the LORD names something else. He says, "I will return to Jerusalem with mercy, and there My house will be rebuilt…" The word is house, friend. The text doesn't mention gates in this promise.

Towers sound impressive, but they aren't in this verse. The LORD says, "I will return to Jerusalem with mercy, and there My house will be rebuilt…" The house is what He names. Stick close to the words and the answer shows up.
It's the other direction, friend. The LORD of Hosts says, "My cities will again overflow with prosperity…" Overflow is the opposite of empty. These are promises of fullness for Judah's cities.

That's right. Here's what the LORD of Hosts says: "My cities will again overflow with prosperity; the LORD will again comfort Zion and choose Jerusalem." Overflowing is the word, and empty isn't. It's like a cookie jar that keeps getting refilled as fast as I empty it.

The LORD says, "the LORD will again comfort Zion and choose Jerusalem." Comfort and choosing come in the same breath. Notice the word "again." He says it will happen again, so I think that makes it sound like coming home.

Leaving is the opposite of what He says. The LORD says, "the LORD will again comfort Zion and choose Jerusalem." And earlier He says, "I will return to Jerusalem with mercy…" (Zechariah 1:16). The LORD is coming back, not walking out.

Testing isn't in this promise. The LORD says, "the LORD will again comfort Zion and choose Jerusalem." To choose something is to pick it, friend, and that's a different thing from putting it through a test. Right beside it, He says, "I will return to Jerusalem with mercy…" (Zechariah 1:16).

The angel says, "These are the horns that have scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem." Scattered means people sent every which way. The horns did that to all three, Judah, Israel and Jerusalem. That's a hard thing to look at, friend, and Zechariah looks right at it.

Guarding would be a kind thing, and that isn't what these horns did. The angel says, "These are the horns that have scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem." Scattering is the opposite of keeping together. That's why the craftsmen are about to show up.

Ruling isn't the word the angel uses. He says, "These are the horns that have scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem." Scattered means sent every which way, friend, and that's a different thing from being ruled.

The LORD says, "…the craftsmen have come to terrify them and throw down these horns of the nations…" Terrify is the first job on their list. The craftsmen have come to do it, and that's after all that scattering.

The craftsmen have come "…to terrify them and throw down these horns of the nations…" Down is where they've come to send them. The nations lifted their horns up against Judah, and the craftsmen have come to throw them down. Different direction, friend.

Polishing is what I'd do with a new stamper, but the craftsmen have a different job. The LORD says they've come "…to terrify them and throw down these horns of the nations…" There's no shining and no buffing. These craftsmen mean business.

Honoring the horns isn't why the craftsmen come. The LORD says they've come "…to terrify them and throw down these horns of the nations…" These horns are the ones that scattered Judah. That's the job the craftsmen have come for.

High is the direction the horns went before. The LORD says the nations "…have lifted up their horns against the land of Judah to scatter it." The craftsmen have come to "…throw down these horns of the nations…" So they've come to send them down, not up.

True. The LORD says, "These are the horns that scattered Judah so that no one could raise his head…" That's a heavy picture, friend. The scattering left no one able to raise his head, and that's why the craftsmen coming matters so much.

The text says it right out. The LORD says, "These are the horns that scattered Judah so that no one could raise his head…" That's a heavy part, friend. The same verse then tells you the craftsmen have come.
